CVE-2026-81497.title: Arbitrary host file read+write via VM template path traversal (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48752)
CVE-2026-81497.description: ### Summary The fix for **CVE-2026-48752** (`GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479`, template-traversal to host read/write, addressed in **7.2.0**) was applied to the **LXC container driver only**. The sibling **QEMU/VM driver's** template path (`driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`) never received the same guard, so its template read and write remain unbounded. An authenticated user who can **create/launch a VM from a custom image**, or **restore a VM backup**, controls the image/backup `metadata.yaml` (the `templates` map and each `tpl.Template` value) and can traverse out of the templates directory to: - **read arbitrary host files** as root, which are then disclosed into the guest, and - **create root-owned files anywhere on the host** (with a `.out` suffix). ### Details The **LXC driver** was hardened for CVE-2026-48752 (`internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go`): ```go os.OpenRoot(d.RootfsPath()) // ~:7493 confines writes if filepath.Base(tpl.Template) != tpl.Template // ~:7515 rejects any '/', blocks all '../' os.Lstat(d.TemplatesPath()) ... ModeSymlink // ~:7519 / ~:7533 rejects symlinked dir/source ``` The **QEMU/VM driver received none of these**. `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow` (func @ `:3712`) has, before its file operations, only a `slices.Contains(tpl.When, trigger)` check. There is **no path validation**: ```go // READ ~:3779 -- raw tpl.Template, no containment tplString, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(d.TemplatesPath(), tpl.Template)) // WRITE ~:3765 -- raw tpl.Template, path is host-side under incusd (root) w, err = os.Create(filepath.Join(path, fmt.Sprintf('%s.out', tpl.Template))) ``` - **READ vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/shadow'` reads an arbitrary host file, which is rendered into the VM config drive (`config/files/*.out`, exported to the guest over 9p/virtiofs) → **host-file disclosure to the attacker's guest**. Cleanest, exact-path vector. - **WRITE vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/cron.d/x'` creates `/etc/cron.d/x.out`, a **root-owned file anywhere on the host** with pongo2-rendered content. A grep for `os.OpenRoot` / `OpenTemplates` over the templates directory in the incus QEMU path returns **zero hits**. Reachability: `templateApplyNow` is invoked from `generateConfigShare` on **VM start**, so the static call path is strong. **Reference remediation.** Apply incus's own LXC-driver guards (the `filepath.Base` reject + `os.OpenRoot` confinement) to `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`, covering both the read and the write. For the **read** specifically, upstream **LXD** is a second reference (it confines the QEMU read via `d.OpenTemplates()`, an `os.Root`). Note that **LXD does *not* confine the QEMU write either**, so the write reference is incus's own LXC guard, not LXD. **Scope / honesty.** Source-confirmed via a white-box review of the public repo at fresh HEAD (`ccdf811`) plus an LXD cross-reference; the guard absence was grep-verified. A live-VM end-to-end PoC is the documented next step. The read is a clean arbitrary host-file disclosure. The write is a genuine root-owned arbitrary-file-create primitive, but the created path is **forced to carry a `.out` suffix**, which constrains a direct write-to-RCE, so this is framed as **High**, not a 9.9 Critical, and no RCE is claimed without a `.out`-compatible execution path. ### PoC On a self-hosted **incus 7.2.0 or later**, craft a VM image whose `metadata.yaml` contains: ```yaml templates: '/x': template: '../../../../../../tmp/incus-poc' when: - start ``` Launch the VM, then confirm on the host: ```bash ls -l /tmp/incus-poc.out # created by incusd (root) = out-of-templates write ``` Separately, a `tpl.Template` of `../../etc/hostname` is read and disclosed into the guest config drive (`config/files/*.out`). ### Impact **Path traversal (CWE-22) + link following (CWE-59)** in the VM/QEMU template path. An authenticated user able to create/launch a VM from a custom image, or restore a VM backup, can: 1. **read arbitrary host files as root**, disclosed into their guest (e.g. `/etc/shadow`), and 2. **create root-owned files** with attacker-controlled content anywhere on the host (`.out`-suffixed). **Undisclosed.** The authoritative public dissection ([Snyk Labs: *Newlines, Symlinks, and Arbitrary Writes: Dissecting High-Severity Vulnerabilities in Incus*](https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/)) covers **only** `driver_lxc.go` and explicitly notes the VM drivers were not separately audited; no incus issue, PR, or CVE names `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`. --- **Reporter:** Kingsley Olukanni (GitHub: **babakizo420**).

GHSA-579w-c4rw-c8q3.title: Arbitrary file write on host via symlink in migration stream
GHSA-579w-c4rw-c8q3.description: ### Summary When receiving an instance or custom storage volume through migration (copy, move, refresh, push or pull), Incus hands the incoming data stream to `rsync`, or to `btrfs receive` for optimized transfers between btrfs pools. Both tools replay the stream on the host using regular path-based system calls and follow symlinks in the paths they write to. A malicious migration source can plant a symlink in the transferred volume, such as `rootfs` pointing at `/`, and have later entries in the same stream (or in the following snapshot or main volume stream) written through it. The symlink check added in Incus 7.3 runs after the transfer, so it doesn't prevent those writes. ### Impact Any client allowed to create an instance or custom volume in a project, or any server a target is told to copy or move from, can write attacker-controlled files to arbitrary paths on the target host as root, leading to full host compromise. For virtual machines the same technique can replace the `root.img` block file with a symlink before the block stream is written through it. All storage drivers receiving through `rsync` are affected, as is the optimized btrfs path. Optimized ZFS transfers are not affected as `zfs receive` never resolves host paths. Releases before 7.3.0 are additionally affected by a `rootfs` symlink surviving the transfer, which the file API then follows when chrooting into the container, allowing host files to be read as well as written. ### Details `rsync` writes each received entry to `<volume>/<path>` and, when the sender marks the parent directories as not transferred, resolves that path through whatever already exists on the receiving side, including a symlink created earlier in the transfer. `btrfs receive` behaves the same way as it applies `mkfile`, `write`, `mkdir` and `rename` commands with plain `creat()`, `open()`, `mkdir()` and `rename()` calls on paths built from the received subvolume. Neither verifies the stream against the real filesystem it was supposed to describe, so a crafted stream isn't constrained to what a genuine sender would produce. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances and custom volumes, and only migrate from trusted servers.

GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup dependent volumes
GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup validates the instance name and snapshot names, but not the names of the dependent custom volumes listed in the backup's `index.yaml`. Those names are used verbatim as path segments when creating the volume on the target storage pool, so a `../` chain escapes the storage pool directory. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can have the Incus daemon create root-owned directories, populated with attacker-controlled content, at arbitrary paths on the host, leading to full host compromise. The backup also names the project each dependent volume is created in, so the same request could create custom volumes in projects the caller has no access to. ### Details The fixes for CVE-2026-81495 and CVE-2026-81496 added name validation to the direct custom volume and instance backup import handlers. The dependent volume path nested inside an instance backup reaches the same volume creation code without going through either check. The name flows through `filepath.Join`, which collapses `../`, into `os.Mkdir` and the subsequent unpacking of the volume data. The attached-device gate can be satisfied by splitting the traversal string across the device's `pool` and `source` fields, as only the pool of the volume entry is resolved against a real storage pool. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances.

GHSA-mfwv-x733-9446.title: Authorization bypass lets a restricted client read any operation in another project
GHSA-mfwv-x733-9446.description: ### Summary **Broken Authorization (CWE-862, Missing Authorization) on `GET /1.0/operations/{uuid}`.** The handler performs no authorization of any kind. Any authenticated client — including a TLS client certificate restricted to a single project — can read the full contents of any in-flight operation in any other project, including the command line, the environment variables and the websocket secrets the operation carries. `operationGet` is registered under `allowAuthenticated`, which your own code documents as deferring the real decision to the handler. The handler never makes one. ### Affected | Line | Range | Verified | |---|---|---| | Feature | `>= v0.2.0`, through `v7.4.0` | runtime, 7.4.0 from your apt repository | | LTS 6.0 | `v6.0.0` – `v6.0.6`, `stable-6.0` HEAD | runtime, 6.0.6 from your apt repository | | 7.0 | `v7.0.0`, `v7.0.1`, `stable-7.0` HEAD | source | | main | `dd19d9938` | source | The check has never existed. `operationGet` is 53 lines with zero authorizer calls at every tag from `v6.0.0` to `v7.4.0` and on all three branch heads. `v0.2.0` is the first release containing `613f937dc`, which is where operations authorization was introduced — so it is the first release in which Incus claims to authorize operations and does not authorize this one. One question on the range rather than an assertion: `doc/support.md` still describes 6.x as the feature line and refers to a future 7.0 LTS, while `stable-7.0` already carries point releases. Please confirm whether 7.0 is a supported line before the advisory range is published. ### Contrast, on one URL, one certificate, one instant A client certificate restricted to project `attacker`. A container `victim-box` in project `victim`. An admin starts an `exec` in `victim` carrying a marker in its environment. Then, as the restricted certificate: ``` --- attacker GET /1.0/operations/7a8fca8a-ff78-49a1-af51-fd73cf56aee1 -> 200 --- attacker GET .../wait?timeout=1 -> 200 --- attacker DELETE /1.0/operations/7a8fca8a-ff78-49a1-af51-fd73cf56aee1 -> 403 --- DELETE error body: {'error_code':403,'error':'User does not have permission for project \'victim\''} --- contents returned by the GET that was allowed, after the DELETE was denied: {'instances':['/1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim']} {'DB_PASSWORD':'s3cr3t-victim-value','HOME':'/root','LANG':'C.UTF-8','USER':'root','PATH':'...'} {'0':'c5c793028efb9e0691423dfcd2a36e6dc18031b1408211ed8aa80308a7aef2a1', '1':'e557d78cd9a22790759e6997f1fdcdb9a5f22c41d811e588a3d96ea9021fffd7', '2':'edf04a0ae7d90ed45e31b322d9be311dfaef2683e5be6676bc07bab34c0caf34', 'control':'afa5bb2ed82f416c563d6f8881a4f5a01c3d66ad14ca3b5ce3f7c90e50c4d85b'} ``` `DELETE` refuses by project. `GET` on the same URL, from the same certificate, in the same second, hands over the victim's command line, environment and websocket secrets. ### Root cause `cmd/incusd/operations.go` registers three actions under `allowAuthenticated`: ```go 33: Delete: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationDelete, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, 34: Get: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationGet, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, 40: Get: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationsGet, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, ``` `cmd/incusd/daemon.go:275` states the contract: > `allowAuthenticated` is an AccessHandler which allows only authenticated requests. This should be used in conjunction with **further access control within the handler** (e.g. to filter resources the user is able to view/edit). Two of the three do that. `operationDelete` resolves the project from `op.Project()`, reads `op.Permission()`, builds an `auth.NewObject` per resource and calls `s.Authorizer.CheckPermission` (`operations.go:280-306`). `operationsGet` takes a `GetPermissionChecker` for `auth.EntitlementCanViewOperations` and filters every local and remote operation through it (`operations.go:538`, `:556`, `:584`). `operationGet` (`operations.go:181`) resolves the operation out of the global UUID-keyed map and renders it: ```go op, err := operations.OperationGetInternal(id) if err == nil { _, body, err = op.Render() if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } return response.SyncResponse(true, body) } ``` No `op.Project()`, no `op.Permission()`, no authorizer call, no read of `?project=`. The map is global, so the UUID alone selects the object. This is not a regression. `git log -S` puts it at the commit that introduced operations authorization: `613f937dc`, 2023-10-25, *'lxd: Update authorization for operations'* — a single-file, 34-line diff with four hunks. One hunk adds the check to `operationDelete`; three add the checker and its two filter sites to `operationsGet`. `operationGet` sits 77 lines above the `operationDelete` hunk **in that same diff** and is not touched. The list and the destructive verb were authorized; the read was walked past. ### Impact A tenant holding a restricted certificate — the mechanism Incus ships specifically to confine a client to its own projects — reads, from any other project on the server: - the full command line of any running `exec`, including anything passed as an argument; - the complete environment of that command, which is where deployment tooling puts database passwords, API tokens and cloud credentials; - the `fds` secrets for the operation's websockets, and the operation's resource URLs, which name instances and volumes in the other project. **Escalation to full server admin, demonstrated.** `incus config trust add` creates a `Running` operation whose metadata *is* the enrolment token. Reading that operation yields the token; the token enrols a fresh, unrestricted client certificate. From the restricted certificate we read such an operation, reassembled the token, enrolled a new certificate, and then read the victim's instance (HTTP 200) and listed every project on the server. We are **not** pricing that chain into the score below, because it needs a trust-token operation to be pending at the moment of the read, and that is operator timing rather than code. It is reported because it bounds what the primitive is worth, not because we are claiming it. **Limitation, stated plainly.** The attacker must know the operation's UUID and cannot get it from Incus. `uuid.New()` (`internal/server/operations/operations.go:138`) is `crypto/rand`-backed UUIDv4, 122 bits. We verified that a restricted certificate sees nothing through any enumeration path: `/1.0/operations?project=attacker`, `?all-projects=true` and `?project=victim` all return empty, and the victim's instance is correctly refused with 403. The UUID must come from outside — an operator's shell history or CI log, the `Location` header of an async response passing through a proxy or APM trace, `incus monitor` output pasted into a ticket, a former project membership, or a co-tenant on a shared automation account. No victim interaction is required after that. This is the same gating you accepted in CVE-2026-81501, whose text reads: *'the 64-hex fingerprint is not returned by GET / list to a caller without CanView. The attacker must obtain it out of band (logs, backups, a former project membership, a predictable custom image, etc.). No victim interaction is required after that.'* ### Suggested fix Give `operationGet` the check `operationDelete` already performs. The finished handler, with the existing body unchanged below it: ```go func operationGet(d *Daemon, r *http.Request) response.Response { s := d.State() id, err := pathVar(r, 'id') if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } var body *api.Operation // First check if the query is for a local operation from this node op, err := operations.OperationGetInternal(id) if err == nil { projectName := op.Project() if projectName == '' { projectName = api.ProjectDefaultName } err = s.Authorizer.CheckPermission(r.Context(), r, auth.ObjectProject(projectName), auth.EntitlementCanViewOperations) if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } _, body, err = op.Render() if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } return response.SyncResponse(true, body) } ``` `CanViewOperations` is the entitlement `operationsGet` already uses for exactly this question, so the read path and the list path end up answering it the same way. Using `op.Permission()` as `operationDelete` does would also work and would be stricter; `CanViewOperations` is suggested because it matches the verb. The cluster-forwarding branch below it inherits the fix for free: the remote member runs `operationGet` too and will apply the same check to the forwarded identity. `operationWaitGet` (`operations.go:46`) is registered `AllowUntrusted: true` and returns the same rendered object on completion. It needs the same treatment or the fix is bypassable by waiting instead of getting. We have not tested that path against a fix and are flagging it rather than asserting it. ### Dedup We could find no published advisory of yours covering operations. The fourteen published between 2026-07-30 and 2026-08-27 are image import, backup import, volume import, cross-project instance copy, migration config override, network address sets, idmap isolation, nvidia capabilities, VM template paths, image symlinks and fingerprints, and a CLI traversal. If this duplicates something already in your queue, please say so and close it — we would rather know than have you carry two. ### PoC Full sequence, reproducible on a clean install. Run as the server admin except where marked. ```sh # --- setup, as admin ------------------------------------------------------- incus project create victim incus project create attacker incus launch images:debian/12 victim-box --project victim # a client certificate restricted to project 'attacker' incus config trust add --name attacker --restricted --projects attacker # enrol that token from the client, then confirm the restriction: incus query /1.0/certificates/<fingerprint> # { 'name': 'attacker', 'restricted': true, 'projects': [ 'attacker' ] } # --- controls: the restriction works --------------------------------------- # as the attacker certificate curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim' # 403 User does not have permission for project 'victim' for q in 'project=attacker' 'all-projects=true' 'project=victim'; do curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations?$q' done # {} {} {} the operation is invisible through every listing curl -k 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # no client cert # 403 # --- the finding ----------------------------------------------------------- # as admin, start a command in the victim project carrying a marker incus exec victim-box --project victim --env DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t-victim-value -- sleep 600 & OPID=$(incus operation list --project victim --format csv | head -1 | cut -d, -f1) # as the attacker certificate, same URL, two verbs curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ -X DELETE 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # 403 User does not have permission for project 'victim' curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # 200, and the body contains: # resources.instances -> /1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim # metadata.environment.DB_PASSWORD -> s3cr3t-victim-value # metadata.fds -> 0, 1, 2, control ``` Verified identically on `7.4.0` and on `6.0.6`, both installed from your apt repository. Both lab containers were destroyed after the run. ### Severity `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` — **6.3 Medium**. This is set to **parity with your own scoring of CVE-2026-81501**, which carries the identical vector, rather than argued upward. Metric by metric: - **AV:N** — the HTTPS API, reachable from wherever the client is. - **AC:H** — the 122-bit UUID must be obtained out of band. This is the metric doing the work, and it is the same one you applied to the out-of-band fingerprint in CVE-2026-81501. - **PR:L** — a valid, enrolled client certificate. Not unauthenticated: `allowAuthenticated` refuses an untrusted client on this URL, and we checked. - **UI:N** — no victim interaction once the UUID is held. - **S:C** — the vulnerable component is the API's authorization layer; the impacted component is another project, which is the isolation boundary Incus sells. - **C:H / I:N / A:N** — the endpoint is read-only. Secrets of arbitrary value are returned. If you prefer to price the demonstrated trust-token chain, the vector becomes `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **8.5 High**. We are not proposing it, for the reason given under Impact, but it is the honest ceiling and the decision is yours.

GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.title: Incus CLI arbitrary file write via malicious incus-agent during recursive file pull
GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.description: ### Summary `incus file pull -r` copies a directory tree out of a virtual machine over SFTP, served by `incus-agent` running inside the guest. The client trusted the agent's directory listing and `Lstat` results without accounting for the fact that a compromised agent can make them inconsistent. A malicious agent can return the same entry name twice, report it as a symlink on the first visit and as a directory or regular file on the second. The client creates the symlink on the first visit and, on the second, recurses into or writes through it, escaping the local target directory. ### Impact An attacker with root inside a virtual machine, running a modified `incus-agent`, can make an operator who runs `incus file pull -r` from that virtual machine write attacker-controlled files, or whole directory trees, to arbitrary paths on the machine running the `incus` CLI, with the operator's privileges. When run as root this allows overwriting files such as `/etc/shadow` or `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The operator has to run a recursive pull from the compromised virtual machine; no other interaction is needed. Containers are not affected as their file transfers are served by `forkfile` on the host rather than by an in-guest agent. ### Details `sftpRecursivePullFile` in `cmd/incus/utils_sftp.go` iterates over the entries returned by `ReadDir`, calls `Lstat` on each and creates the matching local file, directory or symlink under the target. Nothing stopped a later entry from resolving to a path that the transfer itself had just created as a symlink: `os.Mkdir`/`os.Create` follow it, so the 'directory' or 'file' lands wherever the symlink points. ### Workarounds Avoid `incus file pull -r` from untrusted virtual machines, or run it as an unprivileged user into a dedicated directory.

GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.title: Restricted client can read storage bucket keys in the default project
GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.description: ### Summary The storage bucket key endpoints, `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../keys/{key}`, only require `can_view` on the bucket and return the S3 access key and secret key. When using the TLS authorizer, a restricted client certificate is granted read-only access to buckets in the `default` project, so that projects without `features.storage.buckets` can use them. That read-only exception therefore also hands out the bucket credentials. ### Impact A client with a restricted TLS certificate scoped to any project can read the access key and secret key of every bucket in the `default` project, then use them directly against the S3 endpoint to read, modify or delete the objects in those buckets. Only the TLS authorizer is affected. OpenFGA deployments are not. ### Details Bucket keys are credentials rather than metadata, so both key retrieval endpoints now require `can_edit` on the bucket. Listing buckets and reading bucket details remain available under `can_view`. ### Workarounds Don't keep buckets in the `default` project on servers that issue restricted client certificates, or rotate the keys of any bucket a restricted client may have read.

CVE-2026-40243.description:

This issue defeats the intended CA-based trust model for OVN database connections and permits endpoint impersonation by an active attacker in a suitable network position. This issue is fixed in version 7.0.0.

Containers in the project share the host uid/gid map instead of receiving unique, non-overlapping ranges, weakening the isolation boundary between co-tenant containers and the host. Version 7.3.0 patches the issue.

CVE-2026-81497.title: Arbitrary host file read+write via VM template path traversal (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-48752)
CVE-2026-81497.description: ### Summary The fix for **CVE-2026-48752** (`GHSA-vxp5-584q-c479`, template-traversal to host read/write, addressed in **7.2.0**) was applied to the **LXC container driver only**. The sibling **QEMU/VM driver's** template path (`driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`) never received the same guard, so its template read and write remain unbounded. An authenticated user who can **create/launch a VM from a custom image**, or **restore a VM backup**, controls the image/backup `metadata.yaml` (the `templates` map and each `tpl.Template` value) and can traverse out of the templates directory to: - **read arbitrary host files** as root, which are then disclosed into the guest, and - **create root-owned files anywhere on the host** (with a `.out` suffix). ### Details The **LXC driver** was hardened for CVE-2026-48752 (`internal/server/instance/drivers/driver_lxc.go`): ```go os.OpenRoot(d.RootfsPath()) // ~:7493 confines writes if filepath.Base(tpl.Template) != tpl.Template // ~:7515 rejects any '/', blocks all '../' os.Lstat(d.TemplatesPath()) ... ModeSymlink // ~:7519 / ~:7533 rejects symlinked dir/source ``` The **QEMU/VM driver received none of these**. `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow` (func @ `:3712`) has, before its file operations, only a `slices.Contains(tpl.When, trigger)` check. There is **no path validation**: ```go // READ ~:3779 -- raw tpl.Template, no containment tplString, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(d.TemplatesPath(), tpl.Template)) // WRITE ~:3765 -- raw tpl.Template, path is host-side under incusd (root) w, err = os.Create(filepath.Join(path, fmt.Sprintf('%s.out', tpl.Template))) ``` - **READ vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/shadow'` reads an arbitrary host file, which is rendered into the VM config drive (`config/files/*.out`, exported to the guest over 9p/virtiofs) → **host-file disclosure to the attacker's guest**. Cleanest, exact-path vector. - **WRITE vector:** `tpl.Template = '../../../../etc/cron.d/x'` creates `/etc/cron.d/x.out`, a **root-owned file anywhere on the host** with pongo2-rendered content. A grep for `os.OpenRoot` / `OpenTemplates` over the templates directory in the incus QEMU path returns **zero hits**. Reachability: `templateApplyNow` is invoked from `generateConfigShare` on **VM start**, so the static call path is strong. **Reference remediation.** Apply incus's own LXC-driver guards (the `filepath.Base` reject + `os.OpenRoot` confinement) to `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`, covering both the read and the write. For the **read** specifically, upstream **LXD** is a second reference (it confines the QEMU read via `d.OpenTemplates()`, an `os.Root`). Note that **LXD does *not* confine the QEMU write either**, so the write reference is incus's own LXC guard, not LXD. **Scope / honesty.** Source-confirmed via a white-box review of the public repo at fresh HEAD (`ccdf811`) plus an LXD cross-reference; the guard absence was grep-verified. A live-VM end-to-end PoC is the documented next step. The read is a clean arbitrary host-file disclosure. The write is a genuine root-owned arbitrary-file-create primitive, but the created path is **forced to carry a `.out` suffix**, which constrains a direct write-to-RCE, so this is framed as **High**, not a 9.9 Critical, and no RCE is claimed without a `.out`-compatible execution path. ### PoC On a self-hosted **incus 7.2.0 or later**, craft a VM image whose `metadata.yaml` contains: ```yaml templates: '/x': template: '../../../../../../tmp/incus-poc' when: - start ``` Launch the VM, then confirm on the host: ```bash ls -l /tmp/incus-poc.out # created by incusd (root) = out-of-templates write ``` Separately, a `tpl.Template` of `../../etc/hostname` is read and disclosed into the guest config drive (`config/files/*.out`). ### Impact **Path traversal (CWE-22) + link following (CWE-59)** in the VM/QEMU template path. An authenticated user able to create/launch a VM from a custom image, or restore a VM backup, can: 1. **read arbitrary host files as root**, disclosed into their guest (e.g. `/etc/shadow`), and 2. **create root-owned files** with attacker-controlled content anywhere on the host (`.out`-suffixed). **Undisclosed.** The authoritative public dissection ([Snyk Labs: *Newlines, Symlinks, and Arbitrary Writes: Dissecting High-Severity Vulnerabilities in Incus*](https://labs.snyk.io/resources/incus-vulnerabilities-newline-symlink-arbitrary-writes/)) covers **only** `driver_lxc.go` and explicitly notes the VM drivers were not separately audited; no incus issue, PR, or CVE names `driver_qemu.go` → `templateApplyNow`. --- **Reporter:** Kingsley Olukanni (GitHub: **babakizo420**).

GHSA-579w-c4rw-c8q3.title: Arbitrary file write on host via symlink in migration stream
GHSA-579w-c4rw-c8q3.description: ### Summary When receiving an instance or custom storage volume through migration (copy, move, refresh, push or pull), Incus hands the incoming data stream to `rsync`, or to `btrfs receive` for optimized transfers between btrfs pools. Both tools replay the stream on the host using regular path-based system calls and follow symlinks in the paths they write to. A malicious migration source can plant a symlink in the transferred volume, such as `rootfs` pointing at `/`, and have later entries in the same stream (or in the following snapshot or main volume stream) written through it. The symlink check added in Incus 7.3 runs after the transfer, so it doesn't prevent those writes. ### Impact Any client allowed to create an instance or custom volume in a project, or any server a target is told to copy or move from, can write attacker-controlled files to arbitrary paths on the target host as root, leading to full host compromise. For virtual machines the same technique can replace the `root.img` block file with a symlink before the block stream is written through it. All storage drivers receiving through `rsync` are affected, as is the optimized btrfs path. Optimized ZFS transfers are not affected as `zfs receive` never resolves host paths. Releases before 7.3.0 are additionally affected by a `rootfs` symlink surviving the transfer, which the file API then follows when chrooting into the container, allowing host files to be read as well as written. ### Details `rsync` writes each received entry to `<volume>/<path>` and, when the sender marks the parent directories as not transferred, resolves that path through whatever already exists on the receiving side, including a symlink created earlier in the transfer. `btrfs receive` behaves the same way as it applies `mkfile`, `write`, `mkdir` and `rename` commands with plain `creat()`, `open()`, `mkdir()` and `rename()` calls on paths built from the received subvolume. Neither verifies the stream against the real filesystem it was supposed to describe, so a crafted stream isn't constrained to what a genuine sender would produce. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances and custom volumes, and only migrate from trusted servers.

GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.title: Arbitrary file write on host via path traversal in instance backup dependent volumes
GHSA-hpjh-q53p-f27r.description: ### Summary Importing an instance backup validates the instance name and snapshot names, but not the names of the dependent custom volumes listed in the backup's `index.yaml`. Those names are used verbatim as path segments when creating the volume on the target storage pool, so a `../` chain escapes the storage pool directory. ### Impact Any client allowed to create instances in a project can have the Incus daemon create root-owned directories, populated with attacker-controlled content, at arbitrary paths on the host, leading to full host compromise. The backup also names the project each dependent volume is created in, so the same request could create custom volumes in projects the caller has no access to. ### Details The fixes for CVE-2026-81495 and CVE-2026-81496 added name validation to the direct custom volume and instance backup import handlers. The dependent volume path nested inside an instance backup reaches the same volume creation code without going through either check. The name flows through `filepath.Join`, which collapses `../`, into `os.Mkdir` and the subsequent unpacking of the volume data. The attached-device gate can be satisfied by splitting the traversal string across the device's `pool` and `source` fields, as only the pool of the volume entry is resolved against a real storage pool. ### Workarounds Only allow trusted clients to create instances.

GHSA-mfwv-x733-9446.title: Authorization bypass lets a restricted client read any operation in another project
GHSA-mfwv-x733-9446.description: ### Summary **Broken Authorization (CWE-862, Missing Authorization) on `GET /1.0/operations/{uuid}`.** The handler performs no authorization of any kind. Any authenticated client — including a TLS client certificate restricted to a single project — can read the full contents of any in-flight operation in any other project, including the command line, the environment variables and the websocket secrets the operation carries. `operationGet` is registered under `allowAuthenticated`, which your own code documents as deferring the real decision to the handler. The handler never makes one. ### Affected | Line | Range | Verified | |---|---|---| | Feature | `>= v0.2.0`, through `v7.4.0` | runtime, 7.4.0 from your apt repository | | LTS 6.0 | `v6.0.0` – `v6.0.6`, `stable-6.0` HEAD | runtime, 6.0.6 from your apt repository | | 7.0 | `v7.0.0`, `v7.0.1`, `stable-7.0` HEAD | source | | main | `dd19d9938` | source | The check has never existed. `operationGet` is 53 lines with zero authorizer calls at every tag from `v6.0.0` to `v7.4.0` and on all three branch heads. `v0.2.0` is the first release containing `613f937dc`, which is where operations authorization was introduced — so it is the first release in which Incus claims to authorize operations and does not authorize this one. One question on the range rather than an assertion: `doc/support.md` still describes 6.x as the feature line and refers to a future 7.0 LTS, while `stable-7.0` already carries point releases. Please confirm whether 7.0 is a supported line before the advisory range is published. ### Contrast, on one URL, one certificate, one instant A client certificate restricted to project `attacker`. A container `victim-box` in project `victim`. An admin starts an `exec` in `victim` carrying a marker in its environment. Then, as the restricted certificate: ``` --- attacker GET /1.0/operations/7a8fca8a-ff78-49a1-af51-fd73cf56aee1 -> 200 --- attacker GET .../wait?timeout=1 -> 200 --- attacker DELETE /1.0/operations/7a8fca8a-ff78-49a1-af51-fd73cf56aee1 -> 403 --- DELETE error body: {'error_code':403,'error':'User does not have permission for project \'victim\''} --- contents returned by the GET that was allowed, after the DELETE was denied: {'instances':['/1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim']} {'DB_PASSWORD':'s3cr3t-victim-value','HOME':'/root','LANG':'C.UTF-8','USER':'root','PATH':'...'} {'0':'c5c793028efb9e0691423dfcd2a36e6dc18031b1408211ed8aa80308a7aef2a1', '1':'e557d78cd9a22790759e6997f1fdcdb9a5f22c41d811e588a3d96ea9021fffd7', '2':'edf04a0ae7d90ed45e31b322d9be311dfaef2683e5be6676bc07bab34c0caf34', 'control':'afa5bb2ed82f416c563d6f8881a4f5a01c3d66ad14ca3b5ce3f7c90e50c4d85b'} ``` `DELETE` refuses by project. `GET` on the same URL, from the same certificate, in the same second, hands over the victim's command line, environment and websocket secrets. ### Root cause `cmd/incusd/operations.go` registers three actions under `allowAuthenticated`: ```go 33: Delete: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationDelete, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, 34: Get: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationGet, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, 40: Get: APIEndpointAction{Handler: operationsGet, AccessHandler: allowAuthenticated}, ``` `cmd/incusd/daemon.go:275` states the contract: > `allowAuthenticated` is an AccessHandler which allows only authenticated requests. This should be used in conjunction with **further access control within the handler** (e.g. to filter resources the user is able to view/edit). Two of the three do that. `operationDelete` resolves the project from `op.Project()`, reads `op.Permission()`, builds an `auth.NewObject` per resource and calls `s.Authorizer.CheckPermission` (`operations.go:280-306`). `operationsGet` takes a `GetPermissionChecker` for `auth.EntitlementCanViewOperations` and filters every local and remote operation through it (`operations.go:538`, `:556`, `:584`). `operationGet` (`operations.go:181`) resolves the operation out of the global UUID-keyed map and renders it: ```go op, err := operations.OperationGetInternal(id) if err == nil { _, body, err = op.Render() if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } return response.SyncResponse(true, body) } ``` No `op.Project()`, no `op.Permission()`, no authorizer call, no read of `?project=`. The map is global, so the UUID alone selects the object. This is not a regression. `git log -S` puts it at the commit that introduced operations authorization: `613f937dc`, 2023-10-25, *'lxd: Update authorization for operations'* — a single-file, 34-line diff with four hunks. One hunk adds the check to `operationDelete`; three add the checker and its two filter sites to `operationsGet`. `operationGet` sits 77 lines above the `operationDelete` hunk **in that same diff** and is not touched. The list and the destructive verb were authorized; the read was walked past. ### Impact A tenant holding a restricted certificate — the mechanism Incus ships specifically to confine a client to its own projects — reads, from any other project on the server: - the full command line of any running `exec`, including anything passed as an argument; - the complete environment of that command, which is where deployment tooling puts database passwords, API tokens and cloud credentials; - the `fds` secrets for the operation's websockets, and the operation's resource URLs, which name instances and volumes in the other project. **Escalation to full server admin, demonstrated.** `incus config trust add` creates a `Running` operation whose metadata *is* the enrolment token. Reading that operation yields the token; the token enrols a fresh, unrestricted client certificate. From the restricted certificate we read such an operation, reassembled the token, enrolled a new certificate, and then read the victim's instance (HTTP 200) and listed every project on the server. We are **not** pricing that chain into the score below, because it needs a trust-token operation to be pending at the moment of the read, and that is operator timing rather than code. It is reported because it bounds what the primitive is worth, not because we are claiming it. **Limitation, stated plainly.** The attacker must know the operation's UUID and cannot get it from Incus. `uuid.New()` (`internal/server/operations/operations.go:138`) is `crypto/rand`-backed UUIDv4, 122 bits. We verified that a restricted certificate sees nothing through any enumeration path: `/1.0/operations?project=attacker`, `?all-projects=true` and `?project=victim` all return empty, and the victim's instance is correctly refused with 403. The UUID must come from outside — an operator's shell history or CI log, the `Location` header of an async response passing through a proxy or APM trace, `incus monitor` output pasted into a ticket, a former project membership, or a co-tenant on a shared automation account. No victim interaction is required after that. This is the same gating you accepted in CVE-2026-81501, whose text reads: *'the 64-hex fingerprint is not returned by GET / list to a caller without CanView. The attacker must obtain it out of band (logs, backups, a former project membership, a predictable custom image, etc.). No victim interaction is required after that.'* ### Suggested fix Give `operationGet` the check `operationDelete` already performs. The finished handler, with the existing body unchanged below it: ```go func operationGet(d *Daemon, r *http.Request) response.Response { s := d.State() id, err := pathVar(r, 'id') if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } var body *api.Operation // First check if the query is for a local operation from this node op, err := operations.OperationGetInternal(id) if err == nil { projectName := op.Project() if projectName == '' { projectName = api.ProjectDefaultName } err = s.Authorizer.CheckPermission(r.Context(), r, auth.ObjectProject(projectName), auth.EntitlementCanViewOperations) if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } _, body, err = op.Render() if err != nil { return response.SmartError(err) } return response.SyncResponse(true, body) } ``` `CanViewOperations` is the entitlement `operationsGet` already uses for exactly this question, so the read path and the list path end up answering it the same way. Using `op.Permission()` as `operationDelete` does would also work and would be stricter; `CanViewOperations` is suggested because it matches the verb. The cluster-forwarding branch below it inherits the fix for free: the remote member runs `operationGet` too and will apply the same check to the forwarded identity. `operationWaitGet` (`operations.go:46`) is registered `AllowUntrusted: true` and returns the same rendered object on completion. It needs the same treatment or the fix is bypassable by waiting instead of getting. We have not tested that path against a fix and are flagging it rather than asserting it. ### Dedup We could find no published advisory of yours covering operations. The fourteen published between 2026-07-30 and 2026-08-27 are image import, backup import, volume import, cross-project instance copy, migration config override, network address sets, idmap isolation, nvidia capabilities, VM template paths, image symlinks and fingerprints, and a CLI traversal. If this duplicates something already in your queue, please say so and close it — we would rather know than have you carry two. ### PoC Full sequence, reproducible on a clean install. Run as the server admin except where marked. ```sh # --- setup, as admin ------------------------------------------------------- incus project create victim incus project create attacker incus launch images:debian/12 victim-box --project victim # a client certificate restricted to project 'attacker' incus config trust add --name attacker --restricted --projects attacker # enrol that token from the client, then confirm the restriction: incus query /1.0/certificates/<fingerprint> # { 'name': 'attacker', 'restricted': true, 'projects': [ 'attacker' ] } # --- controls: the restriction works --------------------------------------- # as the attacker certificate curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim' # 403 User does not have permission for project 'victim' for q in 'project=attacker' 'all-projects=true' 'project=victim'; do curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations?$q' done # {} {} {} the operation is invisible through every listing curl -k 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # no client cert # 403 # --- the finding ----------------------------------------------------------- # as admin, start a command in the victim project carrying a marker incus exec victim-box --project victim --env DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3t-victim-value -- sleep 600 & OPID=$(incus operation list --project victim --format csv | head -1 | cut -d, -f1) # as the attacker certificate, same URL, two verbs curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ -X DELETE 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # 403 User does not have permission for project 'victim' curl --cert attacker.crt --key attacker.key -k \ 'https://SERVER:8443/1.0/operations/$OPID' # 200, and the body contains: # resources.instances -> /1.0/instances/victim-box?project=victim # metadata.environment.DB_PASSWORD -> s3cr3t-victim-value # metadata.fds -> 0, 1, 2, control ``` Verified identically on `7.4.0` and on `6.0.6`, both installed from your apt repository. Both lab containers were destroyed after the run. ### Severity `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` — **6.3 Medium**. This is set to **parity with your own scoring of CVE-2026-81501**, which carries the identical vector, rather than argued upward. Metric by metric: - **AV:N** — the HTTPS API, reachable from wherever the client is. - **AC:H** — the 122-bit UUID must be obtained out of band. This is the metric doing the work, and it is the same one you applied to the out-of-band fingerprint in CVE-2026-81501. - **PR:L** — a valid, enrolled client certificate. Not unauthenticated: `allowAuthenticated` refuses an untrusted client on this URL, and we checked. - **UI:N** — no victim interaction once the UUID is held. - **S:C** — the vulnerable component is the API's authorization layer; the impacted component is another project, which is the isolation boundary Incus sells. - **C:H / I:N / A:N** — the endpoint is read-only. Secrets of arbitrary value are returned. If you prefer to price the demonstrated trust-token chain, the vector becomes `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` = **8.5 High**. We are not proposing it, for the reason given under Impact, but it is the honest ceiling and the decision is yours.

GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.title: Incus CLI arbitrary file write via malicious incus-agent during recursive file pull
GHSA-wfvq-qh87-gm4j.description: ### Summary `incus file pull -r` copies a directory tree out of a virtual machine over SFTP, served by `incus-agent` running inside the guest. The client trusted the agent's directory listing and `Lstat` results without accounting for the fact that a compromised agent can make them inconsistent. A malicious agent can return the same entry name twice, report it as a symlink on the first visit and as a directory or regular file on the second. The client creates the symlink on the first visit and, on the second, recurses into or writes through it, escaping the local target directory. ### Impact An attacker with root inside a virtual machine, running a modified `incus-agent`, can make an operator who runs `incus file pull -r` from that virtual machine write attacker-controlled files, or whole directory trees, to arbitrary paths on the machine running the `incus` CLI, with the operator's privileges. When run as root this allows overwriting files such as `/etc/shadow` or `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The operator has to run a recursive pull from the compromised virtual machine; no other interaction is needed. Containers are not affected as their file transfers are served by `forkfile` on the host rather than by an in-guest agent. ### Details `sftpRecursivePullFile` in `cmd/incus/utils_sftp.go` iterates over the entries returned by `ReadDir`, calls `Lstat` on each and creates the matching local file, directory or symlink under the target. Nothing stopped a later entry from resolving to a path that the transfer itself had just created as a symlink: `os.Mkdir`/`os.Create` follow it, so the 'directory' or 'file' lands wherever the symlink points. ### Workarounds Avoid `incus file pull -r` from untrusted virtual machines, or run it as an unprivileged user into a dedicated directory.

GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.title: Restricted client can read storage bucket keys in the default project
GHSA-x8gj-2q73-qr6j.description: ### Summary The storage bucket key endpoints, `GET /1.0/storage-pools/{pool}/buckets/{bucket}/keys` and `GET .../keys/{key}`, only require `can_view` on the bucket and return the S3 access key and secret key. When using the TLS authorizer, a restricted client certificate is granted read-only access to buckets in the `default` project, so that projects without `features.storage.buckets` can use them. That read-only exception therefore also hands out the bucket credentials. ### Impact A client with a restricted TLS certificate scoped to any project can read the access key and secret key of every bucket in the `default` project, then use them directly against the S3 endpoint to read, modify or delete the objects in those buckets. Only the TLS authorizer is affected. OpenFGA deployments are not. ### Details Bucket keys are credentials rather than metadata, so both key retrieval endpoints now require `can_edit` on the bucket. Listing buckets and reading bucket details remain available under `can_view`. ### Workarounds Don't keep buckets in the `default` project on servers that issue restricted client certificates, or rotate the keys of any bucket a restricted client may have read.
